title: The Church Bells Still Ring
gist: Marking one year after the Annunciation Catholic Church shooting in Minneapolis, the authors argue the attack was driven not by coherent ideology but by an online 'true crime community' that glorifies mass shooters as 'saints' and pushes teens toward violence for notoriety. They contend the U.S. has no countermessaging or early-intervention infrastructure against this culture, while the FBI now runs more than 250 active investigations into it.

insights.claim: The authors argue the Annunciation shooter's manifesto shows the attack was about notoriety and maximizing suffering rather than any coherent ideology, making the 'nihilistic violent extremism' label too generous.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: If motive is attention-seeking rather than ideology, counterterrorism frameworks built around ideology and legal thresholds will systematically fail to detect or deter these attackers.
insights.quote: It wasn’t for any single ideology, religion, philosophy, or some other tangible or coherent belief: The goal was to create as much suffering as possible in the shortest amount of time.

insights.claim: The FBI defines nihilistic extremism as an ideology aimed at sowing chaos for societal collapse, but the authors say this simplistic gloss credits detached young mass shooters too much because the shooter was no anarchist.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A gap between the FBI's operating definition and the actual phenomenon means official categorization may misdirect resources and prosecution strategy.
insights.quote: giving the attack a simplistic ideological gloss to fit neatly in our preexisting political frameworks credits Westman and other young, detached mass shooters too much.

insights.claim: Inscribed in the chamber of one of the shooter's guns was 'There is no message,' which the authors read as a deliberate attempt to provoke a reaction from everyone about anything or nothing.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The messagelessness is itself the message—an analytic signal that these attackers are optimizing for reaction, which media and platform amplification directly feeds.
insights.quote: In the chamber of a Glock, Westman inscribed, “There is no message.”

insights.claim: An online ecosystem glorifies mass killers as 'saints,' tallies victims in TikTok edits like video-game scores, and pushes members—predominantly teens who call themselves the 'true crime community'—to kill.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Frames radicalization as a peer-driven online subculture rather than lone pathology—implying platform moderation and countermessaging, not just individual mental-health care, are the levers.
insights.quote: an entire online ecosystem glorifies the killers as “saints,” tallying their victims up in TikTok edits like scores in a video game.

insights.claim: The FBI now has more than 250 active investigations into an online culture of death, up from dozens at the time of the August 2025 attack, targeting networks like the true crime community and 764, a group that coerces young people into self-harm and abuse.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A roughly order-of-magnitude jump in active investigations quantifies a fast-scaling threat with younger, more desensitized participants.
insights.quote: Today, the FBI has more than 250 active investigations into an increasingly prevalent online culture of death.

insights.claim: Multiple 2024-2025 shooters shared identical online rituals—Rupnow at Abundant Life, Henderson at Antioch, and Holly at Evergreen used the same three-finger symbol, footwear photos, or a 'Wrath' shirt—evidencing a copycat chain dating to Columbine.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Shared aesthetic markers across attacks give behavioral-threat teams identifiable pre-attack signals to flag online.
insights.quote: Most mass shooting manifestos borrow from the previous ones, in an endless chain of copycat violence dating back to Columbine.

insights.claim: Manifesto content persists on TikTok long after posting—a montage of the Annunciation shooter and the weapons used has stayed on the platform for months while other posts are removed only after a day or two.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Inconsistent enforcement means glorification content stays discoverable for extended periods—a direct platform-accountability failure the authors highlight.
insights.quote: A montage that flashes pictures of Westman and the guns used in the attack, with their chalked words ... has been on the platform for months.

insights.claim: The authors argue most mainstream platforms have ceded moral responsibility for content moderation in favor of bottom lines and a hollow free-expression veneer, while fringe sites intervene even less.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Positions platform economics as an upstream driver of radicalization—relevant to any regulatory or liability shift on content moderation.
insights.quote: Most mainstream platforms have largely ceded their corporate and moral responsibility for policing content on their public squares, in favor of bottom lines and a veneer of protecting free expression that rings hollow upon closer inspection.

insights.claim: 764 and the true crime community cannot be addressed with one-size-fits-all moderation because they are networks of participants adept at flouting algorithmic detection and creating end runs around remedial measures.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Standard automated moderation is structurally insufficient against adaptive networks—implying sustained, human-led intervention is required.
insights.quote: they’re networks of participants who are adept at flouting algorithmic detection and creating end runs around remedial measures.

insights.claim: The U.S. has no government countermessaging campaign or well-funded civil-society effort to push back against violent online extremism, and initiatives to build one were stalled under prior administrations and fully abandoned under the current one.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The absence of any counter-infrastructure is presented as a policy vacuum—a concrete gap where funding or legislation could intervene.
insights.quote: No U.S. government countermessaging campaign or well-funded outside civil society groups exist to push back against this vitriol.

insights.claim: The U.K.'s Channel program, which guides individuals off the radicalization path and saw more than half its referrals last year for children, offers a partial model with no U.S. equivalent.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Points to an existing foreign template for early intervention—useful reference for any U.S. prevention program design.
insights.quote: More than half of the program’s referrals last year were for children.

insights.claim: A patchwork of U.S. states is turning to behavioral threat assessment management teams because much of what these shooters do before attacks never crosses a criminal-charge threshold, but interviews reveal the teams are overworked and woefully underresourced.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The legal-threshold gap forces reliance on under-resourced state teams—identifying where added funding could most affect prevention.
insights.quote: Despite their promising early results, they are overworked and woefully underresourced.

insights.claim: The authors argue Minneapolis's release of 2,648 pages of evidence functioned as a run-of-the-mill document dump, not a true after-action report, with little effort to make sense of the attack or take steps to prevent the next.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Critiques the standard post-incident transparency response as substituting disclosure for prevention analysis—a recurring institutional failure mode.
insights.quote: the release of thousands of pages of public records is no true after-action report.

insights.claim: The authors tie the phenomenon to a cohort that entered adolescence isolated online during the pandemic, when the worst online spaces offered some of the few opportunities to feel connected.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Frames pandemic-era isolation as a structural feeder of radicalization—relevant to understanding the size and durability of the affected cohort.
insights.quote: Many entered their adolescence trapped inside and online as a global pandemic raged outside their windows.

insights.claim: The authors insist attackers are not born idolizing mass shooters but are radicalized by peers into a false sense of belonging, so treating them as unavoidable troubled outliers forecloses prevention.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reframing attackers as radicalized rather than inherently broken is the premise for arguing intervention is possible and worth resourcing.
insights.quote: Westman wasn’t born idolizing mass shooters. Something terrible is happening to our kids, and we seem unwilling to act beyond a passing surface-level self-reflection.
